transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Nice to meet you too, Doctor. Well, to be honest, what brings me in is that I just can't seem to keep my mind on one single thing anymore. It's driving me completely up the wall. I work down at the freight warehouse—I’ve been moving materials and doing inventory there for a while now, and it's a loud place, sure, but lately... lately it's like every little thing completely derails me. 

I'll be right in the middle of a stock count, you know, holding the scanner, going through a massive pallet of boxes, and then, I don't know, a beeper goes off on the other side of the floor, or someone's forklift alarm starts backing up—beep, beep, beep—or even just a coworker dragging a pallet jack two aisles over. And it's like my brain just snaps right over to that noise. I completely lose my place. I'll forget what I was even looking at. Next thing I know, I'm staring at my clipboard and I realize I've put the completely wrong numbers into the inventory system. 

And that's a really big deal, you know, because if the inventory is off, the whole shipping schedule gets messed up, and then my supervisor has to come down and figure out where the discrepancy is, and it's just so frustrating. I used to be able to tune all that out! I even took some college accounting classes years ago, so I know how to focus on numbers and keep things straight. But now, it's just like my attention is being yanked in a hundred different directions the second a single alarm goes off, and I just can't get my work done right.
When you think back to when you were a kid, were you already someone who had a hard time staying focused?

No, no, not at all. Actually, it was quite the opposite when I was younger. I mean, I was the kind of kid who could just sit for hours and get completely lost in a book or a puzzle. My mother used to say she’d have to call my name three or four times just to get me to come down for dinner because I was so zeroed in on whatever I was doing. I remember in middle school—this was back when I was living in Ohio—I had this huge project on the solar system, and I spent an entire weekend just cutting out little foam balls and painting them, completely ignoring the TV and my brothers running around the house. 

And even later, when I took those accounting classes in college, I could sit in the library for hours crunching numbers. I never had a problem with my mind wandering like this. That's why this whole thing at the warehouse is so confusing to me. It's like I'm a completely different person now. I’ve always prided myself on being meticulous, you know? Being the one who catches the little mistakes that other people miss. But now... it’s like my brain just won’t cooperate with what I want it to do, and it’s definitely not something I’ve struggled with my whole life. It really just started recently, this feeling of my attention just slipping away the second there's a distraction.
Did this trouble focusing start after something stressful happened in your life?

Well, I wouldn't necessarily call it a single stressful event, like a car accident or anything dramatic like that, but there has been a big shift at home. It started right about a month ago, maybe exactly four weeks, give or take a couple of days. My husband, Gary—he's always been a real early riser, out the door by 6:00 AM for his job at the hardware store—well, he actually stopped working outside the home. He retired a little earlier than we planned because of some back issues he's been having. 

So, suddenly, he's just... there. All the time. And our whole morning routine, which I've had down to a science for the last fifteen years, is completely upside down. I used to get up, have my coffee in total silence, read a little bit of the paper, and just mentally prepare for the noise at the warehouse. But now, Gary is up, he's puttering around the kitchen, he's asking me where the good coffee filters are, he's turning on the morning news right when I'm trying to think... and it just throws my whole day off before I even leave the driveway. 

And it's been exactly like this for a month now. I leave the house feeling completely scattered, and then I get to work, and it's just like I carry that scattered feeling right onto the warehouse floor with me. It's like my brain gets stuck in this frazzled gear and I just can't shift out of it. I love him to pieces, I really do, but having him home all day has just completely upended everything, and it lines up exactly with when I started messing up all these inventory counts.
Over the past month, have you been feeling down or depressed?

No, I really haven't been feeling down or depressed at all. It's funny you ask that, because my sister, Linda—she lives over in Cincinnati—she called me last week and asked me the exact same thing. She thought maybe I was feeling blue about Gary retiring and being home, like maybe I was mourning the loss of our old routine or feeling old myself, you know, since retirement is such a big milestone. But I told her, and I'll tell you, it's really not that at all. I don't feel sad. I don't feel like crying. I don't have that heavy, dragging feeling you get when you're depressed. 

If anything, I feel the exact opposite of depressed, if that makes sense. I feel like my motor is just running way too fast, not too slow. Like I have all this energy but nowhere to put it, and it just kind of bounces around inside my head and makes me feel completely frazzled. I still enjoy things, you know? I still look forward to my Saturday morning gardening, even if Gary is out there trying to tell me how to prune the hydrangeas now. I still like going to work, even with all the noise and the mistakes I've been making. I'm not dreading getting out of bed or anything like that. It's just this constant, buzzing, scattered feeling. So no, definitely no depression, just a whole lot of frustration that I can't seem to get my brain to settle down and focus on one thing for more than two minutes at a time.
Do you find yourself worrying mainly about the changes since your husband retired and started being home during your mornings?

Well, no, not just that. I mean, yes, the morning routine being completely thrown out the window with Gary being there is a big part of it, absolutely. But it’s not like I’m sitting around wringing my hands, worrying about him being in the kitchen or what he’s doing with his retirement. It’s more like... I’m worrying about everything and nothing all at once, if that makes any sense. 

Like, just yesterday, I was driving to the warehouse, and usually, that’s my time to listen to the local radio station, maybe catch the weather report, just ease into the day. But instead, my mind was racing about whether I remembered to lock the side door of the garage, which I always do, I mean, I’ve never forgotten it in my life. And then I started worrying about the inventory counts at work, not just the ones I messed up, but the ones coming up next week. And then I was thinking about my sister Linda in Cincinnati, and whether I should call her back, and if she thinks I’m going crazy because of how fast I was talking on the phone. 

It’s like my brain is a television remote, and someone is just sitting there flipping through the channels as fast as they can. I can’t just stop on one worry and figure it out. It’s just this constant stream of thoughts—the house, the job, the kids, the dog we haven’t had for five years, just random things popping into my head and making me feel so wound up. So, it’s not just Gary and the mornings. The mornings are just the match that lights the fire, I guess, but once I’m going, I’m worrying about a hundred different things before I even clock in.
Are these worries mostly happening because of the changes since Gary retired?

Well, like I was trying to explain just a minute ago, no, not really. I mean, you would think so, wouldn't you? Because that was the big shift, him being home. But honestly, half the time I’m not even thinking about Gary or his retirement at all when I get like this. He’s doing just fine, actually. He’s taken up fixing all these little things around the house—just yesterday he spent four hours re-caulking the downstairs guest bathtub, which, honestly, didn't even really need it if you ask me, but it keeps him busy and off his feet, which is good for his back. 

So I'm really not worried about him, or the fact that he's retired. It’s more like... my brain just took that one little disruption in my morning coffee routine and decided to just completely short-circuit. The worries aren't actually *about* the changes at home. The changes just... kicked the door open, I guess? And now all these other things are rushing in. Like I said, I'll be worrying about the forklift maintenance logs at the warehouse, or whether I paid the water bill—which I know I did, I always pay it on the second of the month, I have a whole filing system for it in the den—or if I need to get my tires rotated before the winter weather really sets in. It’s just this endless loop of stuff that has absolutely nothing to do with Gary being in the kitchen. So, no, it's definitely not mostly about his retirement. It's just... everything else under the sun.
Have you been feeling this constant worry on most days for at least six months?

Oh, heavens no, not six months. If I had been feeling like this for six months, I think I would have checked myself into the hospital by now! No, it's really only been about a month. It started right around the time Gary officially retired and stopped going to the plant every day. 

I remember the exact week it started, actually, because it was the week after Labor Day. We had that nice long weekend, and then Tuesday rolled around, and normally he'd be up at 5:00 AM, out the door by 5:45, and I'd have the whole kitchen to myself to just sit, drink my Folgers, and read the local section of the paper before I had to get ready for the warehouse. But that Tuesday, he was just... there. Sitting at the island in his bathrobe, wanting to talk about whether we should switch our cable provider. And ever since that week, for the last month or so, it's just been this nonstop buzzing in my head. So no, definitely not six months. Just this past month since our whole morning routine got turned upside down.
